81	## A screener should join four event streams and score three agent populations
82	
83	Everything above converges on a gap no vendor fills for SMBs: enterprise fraud platforms (Signifyd, Riskified, Forter) score at checkout on quote-priced percent-of-GMV contracts, returns platforms (Loop, Narvar) score at the return request, and chargeback tools (Chargeflow at 25% of recovered amounts, $29 per deflected alert) act after the dispute; nothing correlates the three streams for one order or watches for the double-dip and scan-versus-refund timing ([Redo](https://redo.com/resources/articles/comparisons/fraud-platform-pricing); [Redo](https://redo.com/resources/articles/comparisons/chargeback-alternatives-shopify)). A Shopify-plus-Stripe merchant can obtain every input from four sources: Shopify Admin GraphQL (`Order`, `Return`, `ReverseFulfillmentOrder`, `OrderRiskAssessment`, `ShopifyPaymentsDispute`), the Stripe Disputes API with CE 3.0 autofill, carrier tracking APIs (scan events, weight), and support email with photo attachments; the one blind spot is checkout-time IP/device capture, which must be instrumented before the order because Stripe only has what "your integration collects and passes… when your customer makes a payment" ([Stripe](https://docs.stripe.com/disputes/best-practices)).
84	
85	The screener's first module is a per-order **evidence vault** written at checkout, because every rule in the previous two sections rewards pre-sale capture. For human-browser orders it stores `customer_purchase_ip`, a device fingerprint or ID, account ID, email and shipping address in exactly the shapes Stripe's `visa_compelling_evidence_3` sub-fields expect, so the Oct 2026 CE 3.0 autofill and the 24 Oct multi-merchant evidence change work without reconstruction. For agent orders it stores the replacement evidence: the `Signature-Agent` directory and `keyid`, the TAP `idToken` claims (`sub`, `amr`, `auth_time`), the SPT `usage_limits` and `deactivated_reason`, any AP2 mandate hash and UCP agent profile URL, the Mastercard agent flag, the Shopify channel/referrer attribution, and the timestamp and content of the confirmation email, which for ghost orders is "our only window" to the customer ([Shopify Community](https://community.shopify.com/t/agentic-storefronts-your-post-purchase-tools-dont-fire-on-in-chat-checkout-orders-is-anyone-thinking-about-this/592304)). Chargeflow's advice to "log agent-initiated transactions separately" becomes a first-class `agent_population` field with values `signed`, `declared`, `undeclared-suspected` and `human` ([Chargeflow](https://www.chargeflow.io/blog/ai-agent-chargeback-liability)). The `undeclared-suspected` classifier is the technically interesting part: it should combine the Muse fingerprint cluster (identical Linux Chrome hardware/rendering signature across sessions, Cloudflare/Fastly egress ASN, no scroll or hover events, straight-line navigation to checkout, seconds-long sessions) that DataDome and Neos Chronos describe ([DataDome](https://datadome.co/threat-research/meta-muse-doesnt-declare-itself-heres-why-that-matters/); [Neos Chronos](https://neoschronos.com/insights/when-ai-agents-become-the-customer-meta-muse-ecommerce/)) with payment-side tells such as a fresh single-use Link card per order and a name mismatch between order and account ([Alhena](https://alhena.ai/blog/ai-shopping-agent-support-tickets/)). A hackathon verifier for the signed population is small: parse `Signature-Input`, require `tag` in {`web-bot-auth`, `agent-browser-auth`, `agent-payer-auth`}, resolve `keyid` against the `Signature-Agent` directory, Visa's `https://mcp.visa.com/.well-known/jwks` or a UCP profile's `keys[]`, enforce `created`/`expires` and a local nonce store, and verify Ed25519 with Cloudflare's Apache-2.0 `http-message-sig` and `web-bot-auth` npm packages or the Caddy plugin ([GitHub cloudflare/web-bot-auth](https://github.com/cloudflare/web-bot-auth)).
86	
87	The second module scores return requests against a signal taxonomy drawn from what merchants actually catch.
88	
89	| Signal family | Concrete features | Source | Catches |
90	|---|---|---|---|
91	| Customer history | return rate >30–40%, refund-$/order-$ ratio, prior INR/damaged claims, account age, first-order flag | Shopify `Order`/`Return` | Serial abuse, refund-as-a-service |
92	| Order shape | bracketing (multiple sizes/colours of one SKU), high-resale SKU, ship-to ≠ billing, gift-name mismatch | Shopify `Order` | Wardrobing, bracketing, reshipping |
93	| Identity linkage | shared device/IP/address/payment across accounts; relay email domains; agent population | Evidence vault | Multi-account rings, agent relay addresses |
94	| Logistics | carrier scan present/absent, scan-to-refund gap, inbound weight vs SKU weight, label/tracking mismatch, delivery address vs return origin | Carrier tracking API (`weight`, `scanType`, RTS codes) | Empty box, FTID, premature auto-refund |
95	| Claim artifacts | EXIF/metadata, duplicated image regions, generator watermarks, receipt authenticity, physical-plausibility of damage | Return portal/email attachments | AI-generated damage photos, fake drop-off receipts |
96	| Velocity | claims per address/device per 30 days; policy-quote density in claim text; price-drop claims after purchase | Support inbox | Agent-driven "policy lawyer" and price-match sweeps |
97	| Double-dip | open return/refund plus a `Dispute` on the same `charge` | Stripe `Dispute` + Shopify `Return` | Refund-then-chargeback |
98	
99	Each return request should produce a tiered recommendation rather than a binary: instant refund, exchange-first, refund on warehouse inspection, require photo or video verification, or decline with a policy citation. Riskified's "Dynamic Returns" and Signifyd's low/moderate/high scoring already validate tiered treatment commercially ([BusinessWire](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260112619982/en/Riskified-Analysis-Reveals-1-in-4-Refund-Dollars-Is-Abusive-Introduces-Dynamic-Returns-a-New-Policy-Protect-Feature-to-Safeguard-Revenue-While-Increasing-Customer-Satisfaction); [Signifyd](https://www.signifyd.com/news-releases/signifyd-return-abuse-prevention/)), and 56% of consumers say they prefer tiered policies ([BusinessWire](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260622536790/en/Return-Abuse-Goes-Mainstream-as-Nearly-Half-of-Consumers-Use-AI-in-Return-Claims-New-Riskified-Research-Finds)). The recommendation can be pushed into Shopify admin through `orderRiskAssessmentCreate` so staff see `facts[]` next to the order, and through Shopify Flow tags for routing. For agent-originated claims the module should apply the "agent-specific return rules" GSPANN calls for: require the claim to come from the linked customer identity (UCP OAuth link or the original order email), require proof artifacts proportional to the agent population, and refuse automated instant-refund paths that Unit 42's `settlement.refund.instant()` scenario abuses ([GSPANN](https://www.gspann.com/insights/blog/ai-shopping-agents-retailer-terms); [Unit 42](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/retail-fraud-agentic-ai/)).
100	
101	The third module is a **dispute router** whose objective is minimizing VAMP/ECM items, not maximizing wins. On an Ethoca/CDRN alert or a Stripe `warning_needs_response` inquiry, it decides between refund-and-close (removing the item from the VAMP ratio), RDR-style auto-settlement, and representment; it should default to refund for likely friendly fraud on low-ticket orders and to representment only when the evidence vault contains a CE 3.0-qualified match or, for agent orders, a mandate record plus delivery proof. When it represents, it assembles the Stripe `evidence` hash automatically (one merged PDF per evidence type, ≤4.5 MB, 19 pages for Mastercard, full delivery address, policy screenshot as presented at checkout) and stages it with `submit=false` for human review, with the `due_by` deadline surfaced as a countdown ([Stripe](https://docs.stripe.com/disputes/best-practices)). A fourth, smaller module watches for the Rufus pattern on the merchant's own catalog: it diffs what agents could plausibly infer from the product page (fitment, compatibility, size, material) against structured attributes, flags ambiguities like "navy" versus "Midnight" that cause wrong-variant orders ([Alhena](https://alhena.ai/blog/ai-shopping-agent-support-tickets/)), and recommends moving facts into Shopify options or category metafields where agents read them ([Naughton & Bird](https://naughtonandbird.com/signals/shopify-meta-ai-channel-agentic-storefronts)). GSPANN's readiness advice is the same: "write for the constraint the shopper hands the agent, and store every fact where a machine can find it" ([GSPANN](https://www.gspann.com/insights/blog/ai-shopping-agents-retailer-terms)).
102	
103	The tooling gaps to lean on are specific. Neither Shopify nor Stripe documents an "agent-originated" flag on `Order` or `Charge`, so the screener's population classifier is net-new. No Python Web Bot Auth library exists in Cloudflare's repo (TypeScript and Rust only). No vendor offers chargeback liability shift for agent orders, and no evidence format for mandates is accepted in representment, so a screener that stores mandates in a Stripe-evidence-ready shape is ahead of the networks. No per-SKU ground-truth feed to agents exists on Amazon or the open web. And no SMB product joins return, carrier and dispute streams. For a demo, Stripe SPT has a self-serve sandbox, Visa's `trusted-agent-protocol` repo ships a Python agent-registry, tap-agent and merchant-backend plus a Node CDN proxy ([GitHub visa](https://github.com/visa/trusted-agent-protocol)), AP2 has a Python SDK with sample merchant endpoints ([GitHub AP2](https://github.com/google-agentic-commerce/AP2)), and a Shopify dev store exposes the Return, Dispute and risk-assessment APIs. A convincing demo flow runs a signed TAP test agent and an unsigned "Muse-like" Chromium through the same store, shows the vault capturing different evidence for each, replays a double-dip return-plus-dispute, and produces a staged Stripe evidence package with a VAMP-impact estimate.
104	
105	## Conclusion
106	
107	The agent era inverts the merchant's traditional fraud posture. For twenty years the question at checkout was "is this a real cardholder?" and the evidence that answered it (IP, device, session depth) is precisely what Muse and Dots erase, while the question that now decides disputes ("did the human authorize this item, at this price, from this merchant?") has no network-accepted evidence format yet. Merchants were also auto-enrolled into this by Shopify, so the population most exposed to agent-driven returns and "my agent did it" disputes is the sub-$1M store with no fraud platform, which is the exact customer the enterprise vendors do not serve.
108	
109	That makes the screener's real product the evidence vault rather than the scoring model: capturing CE 3.0 elements for humans and mandate/identity records for agents at order time, then spending that evidence in the pre-dispute window where VAMP and Mastercard's ECM actually count. The open question a hackathon cannot settle is whether the networks will carry agent identity into clearing and dispute data; if Visa TAP's `idToken` or AP2 mandates ever appear in representment, the merchants who already stored them per order win immediately, and if they do not, the same vault still turns the only lever merchants control today, refunding before the chargeback is filed, from a guess into a scored decision.

Here is lesson one. It covers the story, the vocabulary judges will use, and the numbers worth memorizing. Read it once, then I'll quiz you or go deeper wherever it's fuzzy.

## The story in four sentences

Shopper agents like Meta Muse and OpenAI Dots now buy things by driving a real Chrome browser in a cloud VM. They do not identify themselves, so to a store they look like a fast human from a data center with no history. The merchant stays the merchant of record, so every wrong order, return, and "my agent did it" chargeback lands on the merchant. Receipts captures the evidence at checkout that agents erase, then uses a team of agents to decide whether to refund early or fight.

## Vocabulary you must own

**Chargeback.** The cardholder calls their bank and says "I dispute this charge." The bank pulls the money back from the merchant. The merchant is guilty until proven innocent.

**Representment.** The merchant fights the chargeback by submitting evidence. Merchants win about 45 percent of fights but net recover only about 11 percent of the money, because fees and labor eat the rest. Stripe says its own win likelihood tops out at 60 percent.

**Friendly fraud.** The real cardholder disputes a legitimate purchase. "I don't recognize this" or "I didn't authorize it." Agents create a new flavor: "my agent did it," which is true, so the customer is not even lying.

**Compelling Evidence 3.0, or CE 3.0.** Visa's rule for beating a fraud dispute. You show two prior undisputed orders from the same customer, 120 to 365 days old, where at least two of account ID, shipping address, IP address, or device fingerprint match, and one match must be IP or device. Agent orders break this because the IP is Cloudflare, the device is a shared VM image, and Muse uses a fresh single-use card each time. So there is no history to match.

**VAMP.** Visa Acquirer Monitoring Program. It counts disputes received, not disputes lost. The threshold dropped to 1.5 percent on April 1, 2026. A withdrawn dispute still counts. The only way to keep an item off the ratio is to refund before the chargeback is filed. This is the whole premise of the pitch line.

**Double-dip.** Customer requests a return, gets auto-refunded when the carrier scans the package, then also files a chargeback on the same charge. It works because refunds release days before the warehouse inspects the box. This is your demo case.

**Evidence vault.** Our per-order record written at checkout. For humans it stores IP, device, account, email, address in the exact field shapes Stripe expects. For agents it stores signature key ID, token claims, spend limits, and the mandate record. The vault is the real product. The agents just spend what the vault captured.

**Three populations.** Signed agents prove identity with a cryptographic key. Declared agents announce themselves with a user-agent string and IP list. Undeclared agents hide in real browsers. Muse and Dots are undeclared. Only behavior signals catch them today.

**Web Bot Auth.** The IETF draft from Cloudflare and Google. Agents sign requests with Ed25519 keys and publish them at a well-known URL. Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol reuses it with different tags and adds a token saying how the human authenticated. Our verifier checks these. Muse and Dots do not sign.

## Numbers for the stage

| Fact | Number |
|---|---|
| Muse launched | Sept 8, 2026, number one US app by Sept 18 |
| Dots launched | Sept 29, 2026 |
| Amazon blocked Muse | Sept 20 to 21, 2026 |
| Merchants who can identify agent traffic | 23 percent |
| US returns in 2025 | $850B, 9 to 15 percent fraudulent, about $100B |
| Consumers using GenAI to draft return claims | 50 percent |
| VAMP threshold | 1.5 percent since April 1, 2026 |
| Merchants who win but net recover | 45 percent win, 11 percent recovered |
| Merchants who think AI providers should be liable | 93 percent |
| One AI photo fraud ring took | $800,000 |

## The one quote to use

DataDome on Muse: "no custom User-Agent, no declared header that says an AI agent is driving this session." Every Muse session looks like "an entirely unremarkable desktop Chrome browser on Linux."

## Hard questions you will get

**"Does any agent actually sign today?"** No. Muse and Dots do not. OpenAI's older Operator did in 2025. Visa's protocol and Cloudflare's verified bots exist in production. We built for where the rails are going and handle today's undeclared traffic with behavior signals.

**"Why not just block agents?"** Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora and Gap signed on as Muse partners. Blocking loses sales silently. Over-blocked agents do not complain, they just do not convert. One audit found 35 percent of agent-ready stores never reach checkout.

**"Why five agents instead of one?"** Each specialist has different data: order history, carrier scans, identity linkage, photo forensics. The critic scores them so one hallucination does not decide a refund. The room is also the audit trail, which matters when you later show a bank why you refunded.

**"Who is the customer?"** The sub-million-dollar Shopify store. Signifyd and Riskified only sell to enterprises on percent-of-revenue contracts. Chargeflow takes 25 percent of recoveries. Nobody joins orders, returns, carrier data and disputes for one order at SMB scale.

**"Is this real or anticipated?"** Honest answer: no public report yet of a Muse or Dots order being charged back. Checkout has been live under two weeks. The proven version is Amazon Rufus, where sellers lose claims because the AI said an item fits. Muse and Dots are the accelerant.

Next lesson when you want it: how the Stripe dispute object and evidence hash work, the verdict tiers the critic returns, and how to walk through the demo in 90 seconds.

# Receipts

> The shopper now has an agent. Meta Muse and OpenAI Dots arrive at checkout as plain Chromium

1. **Evidence vault at checkout.** Every order is classified into a population using only what the
   merchant observed at checkout: `signed` (Web Bot Auth signature verified against the agent's key
   directory, Visa Trusted Agent Protocol token, shared payment token, mandate), `declared`
   (`Agent/` user agent, no signature), `undeclared-suspected` (Muse-like: a sandbox fingerprint shared
   by dozens of sessions, Cloudflare or Fastly egress, zero pointer telemetry, straight-line checkout,
   single-use Link card) or `human`. The vault stores CE 3.0 fields for humans and the replacement
   identity evidence for agents, plus delivery proof, policy snapshot and confirmation email.
2. **Signed-agent verifier.** An Express middleware implementing the IETF Web Bot Auth draft on
   RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures: parses `Signature-Input`, `Signature`, `Signature-Agent`, resolves
   the key id against `/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory`, enforces `created` / `expires`
   and a nonce store, verifies Ed25519. Test clients play a signed agent, a Muse-like unsigned
   browser and a human against the same checkout.
3. **War room.** A return request or Stripe dispute opens a case. Five ZooWork agents, each bound to
   a Band identity, coordinate in a Band room: the Critic posts the brief and @mentions History,
   Logistics, Identity and Forensics; each pulls evidence with its own tools, attaches findings to the
   case file and replies through the room; the Critic weighs everything and issues a tiered verdict:
   instant refund, exchange first, refund on inspection, require verification, or decline with a policy
   citation.
4. **Dispute router.** For disputes it optimises Visa VAMP exposure rather than win rate: refund and
   close an inquiry when that is cheaper than a VAMP item, represent when the vault holds a prior
   refund plus delivery proof, CE 3.0 qualifying history, or a passkey-authenticated agent token. When
   it represents, it creates the dispute in Stripe test mode and stages the evidence package with
   `submit=false`, so a human approves in the dashboard.
5. **Exhibit.** A three.js force graph of orders, customers, devices, addresses, cards, returns and
   disputes. Agents fly to the case node and attach evidence live; ring clusters pull together; the
   side panel shows the transcript, verdict, routing, VAMP arithmetic and the staged Stripe package
   with a countdown to the evidence deadline.

| Piece | Technology |
|---|---|
| Agents | [ZooWork Managed Agents](https://zoowork.ai) via `@zoowork-ai/sdk`: five agents with application-executed custom tools over the vault |
| Coordination | [Band](https://band.ai) rooms and @mentions through the Agent REST API; five registered Band identities |
| Build provenance | [Entire](https://entire.io) mirrors the repo and attaches every Claude Code session to its commits |
| Payments | Stripe test mode: disputes created with `pm_card_createDispute`, evidence staged unsubmitted |
| Verifier | `web-bot-auth` and `http-message-sig` (Cloudflare, Apache-2.0), Ed25519 via Node crypto |
| Exhibit | three.js, 3d-force-graph, UnrealBloomPass, Vite |
| Data | Deterministic seeded dataset: 236 orders, 75 customers, 38 returns, 10 disputes, planted abuse patterns |

Yes, that is the right tier, and it is the one I would defend hardest on stage.

**Why refund on inspection beats the two neighbors**

- **Not decline.** Declining a first-order human with no ring linkage invites a product-unacceptable chargeback. That dispute counts toward VAMP whether you win or lose. Keeping the claim inside the returns flow keeps it off Visa's ledger. This is exactly the "minimize disputes received, not maximize wins" logic the router is built on.
- **Not instant refund or exchange.** The photos are the only damage evidence and they are fabricated. Two generator watermarks is near-conclusive, missing EXIF and duplicated regions corroborate it. Paying out on that, and waiving the return as the customer demands, is the exact pattern that cost one merchant $800,000.
- **Refund on inspection** forces the item back. If it is genuinely damaged, the customer loses nothing but a few days. If it is fine, the claim either dies or becomes an ordinary change-of-mind return under the 30-day policy.

**The customer's own legal argument supports the verdict.** They cited the Consumer Rights Act. Under that act the consumer must make the goods available for return, and the refund is due after the trader receives them. So "refund without return shipping" is not a right the act grants, and the verdict is compliant with the law the customer invoked. One wrinkle: if the item really is faulty, the act puts return postage on the merchant. So the correct operational move is to issue a return label, inspect, then decide who eats the postage. That matches the tier.

**Two refinements, neither urgent**

- The rationale could name the fork: if the item returns undamaged, reclassify as change-of-mind and apply the standard return fee. That shows the judge the tier is a process, not a stall.
- Given the fabrication evidence, the account deserves a tag for future velocity checks even though no ring linkage exists today. A one-liner in the critic's output would do it.

**How to say it to a judge in one breath:** "The photos are AI-generated, so we will not pay on them. But the customer is a human with no abuse history, so we do not decline either, because a decline becomes a chargeback and chargebacks count against us even when we win. We ask for the item back. That costs the honest customer three days and costs the fraudster the whole scheme."

Confidence at 97 percent reads right for this evidence. It would be too high if the photos were merely EXIF-stripped, which happens with ordinary phone uploads. The watermarks are what justify it.
